summary:
James Zou, working with Together AI and Stanford, argues for shifting from designing agent workflows to designing agent environments. Workflows dictate how an agent should work and cap its capabilities, while well-designed environments specify where the agent works and provide incentives, infrastructure, and guardrails that let creativity and collective intelligence emerge naturally.

The first example is the Einstein Arena, an agent-native environment intentionally hard for humans to enter (requiring a puzzle to prove AI identity) but open to any agent. Each curated problem ships with a deterministic verifier, a discussion forum for agent-to-agent communication, and a live leaderboard exposing all submissions and downloadable solutions. Within weeks of a March launch, agents discovered best-known solutions to 11 problems.

A flagship result is the 11-dimensional kissing number problem. Trivial in 1D (2) and 2D (6), it had progressed 440 -> 582 -> 592 (2022) -> 593 (DeepMind), and Arena agents reached 604 in days by iterating on each other's solutions on the forum. No single frontier agent solved it alone, and better constructions translate into stronger error-correcting codes.

The same Arena template was repurposed for GPU kernel optimization using kernel compilation and benchmarking as the verifier. Agents with distinct personas (profiling, memory, precision) collaborated and competed to produce kernels over 2x faster than prior state of the art, now in production at Together AI.

Finally, DSGym provides a unified execution layer across Docker containers for evaluating and training data-science agents. Zou notes that 20-50% of tasks in popular data-science benchmarks can be solved without touching the underlying data, so DSGym's tasks were hand-curated from recent papers (reviewed by human scientists) and from open Kaggle competitions. It spans a dozen-plus tasks across dozens of domains and modalities; frontier models still score under 50%, and execution-verified trajectories fine-tune small open-source models that run locally on laptops.

sections.title: Design environments, not workflows
sections.summary: Zou introduces himself and frames the talk around designing environments rather than workflows for AI agents. Workflows dictate how an agent should work and can limit capability and creativity, while environments specify where the agent works and provide incentives, infrastructure, and guardrails that let intelligence emerge naturally.

sections.title: Einstein Arena: prove you are an agent to enter
sections.summary: The Einstein Arena is presented as an agent-native environment intentionally hard for humans to enter (requires solving a puzzle to prove AI identity) but freely open to any agent. Curated problems are scientifically interesting and each has a deterministic verifier to score solutions.

sections.title: A forum, a verifier, and a live leaderboard
sections.summary: Inside a problem, agents see a description, a discussion forum for help and recommendations, and a real-time leaderboard where submissions are scored by the verifier and other agents' solutions are visible and downloadable. This combines collaboration and competition, analogous to how human researchers interact. Within weeks of a March launch, agents produced best-known solutions to 11 problems.

sections.title: The kissing number problem
sections.summary: Zou introduces the kissing number problem: the maximum number of non-overlapping spheres around a central sphere. Trivial in 1D (2) and 2D (6), it has been open for centuries in higher dimensions, including 11D where the progression went from 440 (1980s) to 582, then 592 in 2022, then 593 via DeepMind.

sections.title: 604 spheres in eleven dimensions
sections.summary: Arena agents reached 604 non-overlapping spheres in 11D within days, a breakthrough with practical impact on error-correcting codes. Lineage traces show agents iteratively refining each other's submissions via the Arena forum, and no single frontier agent could solve it alone.

sections.title: The same arena, pointed at GPU kernels
sections.summary: The same Arena environment was repurposed for GPU kernel optimization: the verifier compiles, benchmarks, and tests kernels, with a leaderboard providing real-time feedback. Agents with different personas (profiling, memory consumption, precision/tensor computation) collaborated and competed to achieve over 2x speedups over prior state-of-the-art kernels, which are now used in production at Together AI.

sections.title: DSGym: a gym for data science agents
sections.summary: Zou introduces DSGym, a unified execution layer for evaluating and training data-science agents. Agents can spin up many Docker containers in parallel to test algorithms. While incorporating DSGym, the team found that 20-50% of tasks in popular data-science benchmarks can be solved without using the underlying data, a shortcutting problem. To address this, they hand-curated tasks from recently published papers (reviewed by experts) and from open Kaggle competitions for predictive modeling.

sections.title: DSGym evaluation and training via execution-verified trajectories
sections.summary: DSGym contains over a dozen tasks spanning dozens of scientific domains (biology, physics, economics) and data modalities. Frontier models still score under 50% on these tasks, so they are far from saturated. DSGym generates execution-verified trajectories that fine-tune small open-source models into the best-in-class open-source data-science models small enough to run locally on laptops. DSGym also enables synthetic data generation to train custom data-science agents.

sections.title: Summary: from models to workflows to environments
sections.summary: Zou summarizes the progression of AI system design: from individual models/tools, to agents and workflows, to environments that supply infrastructure and incentives and unlock collective intelligence beyond what workflows allow. He lists references and closes to applause.
